claim: Antarctic krill has an estimated biomass of 300–500 million tons.

claim: Antarctic krill is among the most abundant wild species worldwide.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bar On et al., 2018.

claim: Antarctic krill is an important prey for predators such as whales, seals, and penguins.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Trathan et al., 2016.

claim: Antarctic krill's huge abundance and central position in the food web makes it a key species of fundamental importance for the functioning of the Southern Ocean ecosystem.
source: Its huge abundance and central position in the food web makes krill a key species of fundamental importance for the functioning of the Southern Ocean ecosystem (Cavan et al., 2019; Trinh et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cavan et al., 2019 and Trinh et al., 2023.

claim: Krill is mostly found in swarms, the largest of which can be hundreds of meters long and tens of meters in height.
source: Krill is mostly found in swarms, the largest of which can be hundreds of meters long and tens of meters in height, likely reflecting a behavioral adaptation to minimize the risk of predation (Tarling et al., 2009; Hamner and Hamner, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tarling et al., 2009 and Hamner and Hamner, 2000.

claim: Krill swarming behavior likely reflects a behavioral adaptation to minimize the risk of predation.
source: Krill is mostly found in swarms, the largest of which can be hundreds of meters long and tens of meters in height, likely reflecting a behavioral adaptation to minimize the risk of predation (Tarling et al., 2009; Hamner and Hamner, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tarling et al., 2009 and Hamner and Hamner, 2000, and involves speculative reasoning about the adaptive function of swarming.

claim: Krill display diel vertical migration (DVM), a common behavior among many pelagic zooplankton organisms across different taxa found in all oceans.
source: Along with their pronounced swarming behavior, krill display diel vertical migration (DVM), a common behavior among many pelagic zooplankton organisms across different taxa found in all oceans (Bandara et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bandara et al., 2021.

claim: DVM is commonly characterized by an ascent to the surface layers in the dark of the night to feed and a descent to darker parts of the water column during the day to avoid visually hunting predators.
source: DVM is commonly characterized by an ascent to the surface layers in the dark of the night to feed and a descent to darker parts of the water column during the day to avoid visually hunting predators (Bandara et al., 2021; Hays, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bandara et al., 2021 and Hays, 2003.

claim: The regular, synchronized movement of krill's large biomass significantly shapes the structure of ecosystems.
source: The regular, synchronized movement of this large biomass significantly shapes the structure of ecosystems (Nichols et al., 2022) and has large impacts on biogeochemical cycles (Aumont et al., 2018; Archibald et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nichols et al., 2022.

claim: The regular, synchronized movement of krill's large biomass has large impacts on biogeochemical cycles.
source: The regular, synchronized movement of this large biomass significantly shapes the structure of ecosystems (Nichols et al., 2022) and has large impacts on biogeochemical cycles (Aumont et al., 2018; Archibald et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aumont et al., 2018 and Archibald et al., 2019.

claim: Krill DVM impacts include the recycling of nutrients, stimulation of primary production, as well as transport and storage of carbon in the deep ocean.
source: This includes the recycling of nutrients, stimulation of primary production, as well as transport and storage of carbon in the deep ocean (Cavan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cavan et al., 2019.

claim: A 'regular' DVM pattern has been commonly observed for krill swarms.
source: Although such a 'regular' DVM pattern has been commonly observed for krill swarms (Godlewska, 1996; Everson, 1983), there is considerable behavioral variation, including reverse DVM, higher frequency migrations, or no synchronized migrations at all (Godlewska, 1996; Bahlburg et al., 2023b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Godlewska, 1996 and Everson, 1983.

claim: There is considerable behavioral variation in krill DVM, including reverse DVM, higher frequency migrations, or no synchronized migrations at all.
source: Although such a 'regular' DVM pattern has been commonly observed for krill swarms (Godlewska, 1996; Everson, 1983), there is considerable behavioral variation, including reverse DVM, higher frequency migrations, or no synchronized migrations at all (Godlewska, 1996; Bahlburg et al., 2023b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Godlewska, 1996 and Bahlburg et al., 2023b.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of DVM and its modulations are not understood.
source: While the adaptive advantage of balancing increased predation pressure during the day with the need to feed seems obvious, the underlying mechanisms of DVM and its modulations are not understood.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Light is thought to be the most reliable and thus important environmental cue for DVM.
source: Light is thought to be the most reliable and thus important environmental cue for DVM (Ringelberg and Van Gool, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ringelberg and Van Gool, 2003.

claim: A study in the marine copepod Calanus finmarchicus indicates that DVM behavior is underpinned by a circadian clock.
source: However, a study in the marine copepod Calanus finmarchicus indicates that DVM behavior is underpinned by a circadian clock, which helps the animals to adjust behavior, physiology, and gene expression to the day-night cycle (Häfker et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Häfker et al., 2017.

claim: A study on Norwegian krill, Meganyctiphanes norvegica, suggested swimming activity in krill is under clock control, with increased activity during the dark phase.
source: Similarly, a study on Norwegian krill, Meganyctiphanes norvegica, suggested swimming activity in krill is under clock control, with increased activity during the dark phase (Velsch and Champalbert, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Velsch and Champalbert, 1994.

claim: Previous studies on Antarctic krill gave first hints that daily behavioral activity in krill is partly under endogenous control.
source: In Antarctic krill, similar studies have been conducted to test the hypothesis of a clock involvement in DVM behavior (Gaten et al., 2008; Piccolin et al., 2020). While these studies gave first hints that daily behavioral activity in krill is partly under endogenous control, a large variability hindered a clear characterization of the circadian behavioral activity of krill.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gaten et al., 2008 and Piccolin et al., 2020.

claim: Previous studies identified the molecular components of a krill circadian clock.

claim: The krill circadian clock drives daily rhythms in gene expression, metabolism, and behavior.

claim: Part of krill's success lies in its strong adaptation to the extreme seasonality of the Southern Ocean environment.

claim: Photoperiod is a major driver for seasonal ecophysiological changes in krill.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2011, Höring et al., 2018, and Teschke et al., 2007.

claim: It has been suggested that an endogenous timekeeping system (i.e. biological clock) is involved in krill seasonal changes, which uses photoperiod as a synchronizing cue.
source: Results from laboratory studies showed that photoperiod is a major driver for seasonal ecophysiological changes in krill (Brown et al., 2011; Höring et al., 2018; Teschke et al., 2007), and it has been suggested that an endogenous timekeeping system (i.e. biological clock) is involved, which uses photoperiod as a synchronizing cue (Höring et al., 2018; Piccolin et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Höring et al., 2018 and Piccolin et al., 2018b.

claim: Circadian clocks are widespread and well-studied endogenous timing mechanisms which allow an organism to fine-tune biological functions to specific times of the day-night cycle.
source: Circadian clocks are widespread and well-studied endogenous timing mechanisms which allow an organism to fine-tune biological functions to specific times of the day-night cycle.

claim: The endogenous oscillation of circadian clocks is produced by transcriptional-translational feedback loops of a set of clock genes and their translation products.
source: The endogenous oscillation is produced by transcriptional-translational feedback loops of a set of clock genes and their translation products (Tomioka and Matsumoto, 2010), which, under the absence of external cues, produce a temporal signal with a period (τ) of about 24 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tomioka and Matsumoto, 2010.

claim: Under the absence of external cues, circadian clocks produce a temporal signal with a period (τ) of about 24 hr.
source: The endogenous oscillation is produced by transcriptional-translational feedback loops of a set of clock genes and their translation products (Tomioka and Matsumoto, 2010), which, under the absence of external cues, produce a temporal signal with a period (τ) of about 24 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tomioka and Matsumoto, 2010.

claim: Under natural conditions, the rhythm of the central oscillator is synchronized to exactly 24 hr by predictable environmental cycles, called zeitgeber, of which light is usually the most important.

claim: The circadian clock allows organisms to anticipate daily environmental cycles and adapt their biology, ultimately increasing survival and fitness.

claim: An understanding of the mechanistic underpinnings of biological timing is essential to comprehend how organisms adapt to their specific environment.
